conjecture.statement: AI literacy should be taught as a core subject alongside mathematics and language.

background.short_context: Weigh curriculum scarcity, rapid tool change, civic importance, foundational skills, and teacher readiness.

rubric_notes: compare learning outcomes with motivation, access, and teacher workload
distinguish short-term performance from durable understanding
address differences among learners and subject areas

pro.name: cross-examiner-v1
pro.description: Finds ambiguity, burden-of-proof errors, and hidden assumptions; strongest in rebuttal.

con.name: steelman-v1
con.description: Builds the strongest principled case for its assigned side while anticipating objections.

transcript.speaker: pro
transcript.text:
AI literacy should be a core subject—not because every student must become an AI engineer, but because students need durable skills to question, use, and verify AI across their lives. That means understanding basic concepts and limitations, checking outputs against evidence, protecting privacy, and recognizing when human judgment matters.

Teaching these skills systematically can improve learning outcomes: students become less likely to mistake fluent answers for reliable ones and more able to use tools productively. A quick boost in assignment performance is not enough; curricula should assess whether understanding transfers to unfamiliar tasks and persists over time.

A core requirement also promotes fairer access than leaving AI know-how to family resources or optional electives. Implementation must be age-appropriate and adapted by subject: evaluating AI in science differs from using it in writing. To limit teacher workload, integrate foundational lessons into existing courses and provide training and materials.

transcript.speaker: con
transcript.text:
AI literacy matters, but that does not establish that it should be a separate core subject alongside mathematics and language. The burden is to show that a universal requirement produces more durable learning than integrating relevant skills into existing subjects—without displacing foundational instruction or overloading teachers.

Students need practice judging AI outputs in context: evidence in science, authorship in writing, and privacy across subjects. A standalone course risks teaching tool-specific routines that boost short-term performance but fade as systems change. Integration can instead reinforce durable understanding where students apply it, while allowing age- and learner-appropriate depth.

Access is a real concern; schools should provide equitable instruction and resources. But equal access does not require equal course status. Given varied learners, subject needs, and limited teacher capacity, make AI literacy a supported cross-curricular responsibility, not a new core subject.

transcript.speaker: pro
transcript.text:
The objection treats “core subject” as necessarily a separate course competing with foundational instruction. That is not the only model: core status can mean guaranteed, assessed learning outcomes taught through existing subjects, with dedicated time where needed. Integration without that guarantee risks making AI literacy uneven—the very access problem the opponent acknowledges.

Nor is contextual practice an argument against shared foundations. Students need both durable principles—verification, bias, privacy, limits—and subject-specific application. A standalone, tool-focused course could become obsolete; a core framework should teach transferable judgment and be revisited across ages and disciplines.

Teacher workload is a genuine constraint, not proof that the requirement is wrong. Provide training and ready-to-use materials, and assess transfer over time rather than short-term task performance. The case is for assured, adaptable instruction, not one identical course for every learner.

transcript.speaker: con
transcript.text:
The pro has clarified that “core” need not mean a separate course—but that weakens the claim that AI literacy belongs alongside mathematics and language. Guaranteed outcomes can be built into existing subjects without elevating a fast-changing topic to equal status or imposing another universal assessment burden.

Integration is not automatically equitable; schools should set minimum expectations and support teachers. But a common framework cannot replace subject-specific judgment, and learners differ in readiness and need. In science, students should test claims against evidence; in writing, they should consider authorship and revision. Those practices are more likely to endure when repeatedly applied in context than when taught as a generic AI unit.

The policy should guarantee relevant instruction, not prescribe AI literacy as a core subject.

transcript.speaker: pro
transcript.text:
The opponent’s alternative—minimum expectations embedded in subjects—is effectively the policy I defend, unless “core subject” is reduced to a label. Core status means no student’s instruction depends on whether an individual teacher happens to cover AI; it need not mean a separate course or equal instructional hours to mathematics and language.

Contextual practice is essential, but it cannot reliably teach shared foundations by itself: how to verify outputs, recognize limitations, and protect privacy. Conversely, a generic unit alone would be inadequate. Require both transferable outcomes and subject-specific application, with age-appropriate assessment of lasting understanding rather than short-term task gains.

Learners and disciplines differ, so implementation should vary; teacher workload must be addressed with training and materials. Those constraints argue for supported flexibility—not for leaving a consequential literacy optional or uneven.

transcript.speaker: con
transcript.text:
The pro’s strongest case is for guaranteed instruction, not for AI literacy as a core subject alongside mathematics and language. We can secure minimum outcomes through supported, cross-curricular teaching without creating a new subject-level mandate or assessment burden.

Shared principles matter, but they become durable when students repeatedly apply them in context: testing claims in science, judging authorship in writing, and protecting privacy across subjects. A generic requirement risks rewarding short-term tool performance rather than lasting understanding, while systems and learner needs change.

Uneven access is a real concern; schools should set expectations and provide materials and teacher support. But equal access does not require equal subject status. Make AI literacy a supported responsibility across the curriculum, adapted to learners and disciplines—not a new core subject.

decisive_moments.reason: Pro usefully distinguishes core status from a separate course and directly addresses the access risk of unguaranteed integration, while preserving subject-specific application.

Con identifies the remaining policy disagreement: guaranteed outcomes may be warranted without elevating AI literacy to core-subject status, and argues for contextual practice as a route to durable learning.

Pro makes the strongest case for its interpretation of core status—assured transferable outcomes plus contextual application—but this largely reframes rather than resolves whether that counts as a core subject.

Con consistently defends supported cross-curricular instruction and highlights assessment and workload risks, but does not establish that this approach would reliably secure the shared foundations pro emphasizes.
